transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. What brings you in to see me?

Well, thanks for seeing me, doctor. I guess... what really brings me in is this feeling I just can't seem to shake. I work as a building cleaner, mostly doing the floors at the local community college, which is usually great because I'm always on my feet, walking the halls, emptying bins, keeping busy. I've always liked working with my hands. But whenever I'm actually supposed to just sit still—like when my supervisor makes us come in for those mandatory monthly staff meetings, or even on weekends when I'm at church and we have these long event briefings for the volunteer team—it’s just... it's unbearable. 

I feel like I’ve got this literal motor humming right under my skin. It's like a physical vibration, you know? I try to just sit there in those uncomfortable plastic folding chairs and pay attention to whoever is talking, but I end up shifting my weight constantly, crossing and uncrossing my legs, tapping my boots, and eventually, I just have to stand up. I always end up finding some excuse to move around the room. I'll get up and pretend I need to check the thermostat, or I'll say I need to throw a wrapper in the trash, or I'll go get a third cup of coffee that I don't even really want, just so I have a reason to walk to the back of the room and pace a little. It’s just this constant, humming energy, and it’s getting to the point where people are starting to look at me funny because I just can't stay planted in a chair for twenty minutes like everybody else seems to be able to do.
Are you currently taking, or have you recently started, any new medications—especially antipsychotics or anti-nausea drugs?

No, no, I'm not taking anything like that. Actually, I'm not really a big pill guy to begin with, you know? The only thing I ever really take is maybe an ibuprofen if my knees are acting up after a long shift of buffering the floors—those machines can really pull on your joints if you're not careful, and at my age, you definitely feel it the next morning. But as for the things you mentioned, antipsychotics or anti-nausea stuff, no, definitely not. I mean, I haven't been sick to my stomach in years, thank the Lord, because working around the chemicals and the smells in the bathrooms at the college is hard enough without having a weak stomach. And I don't even go to the doctor that often, to be honest with you. My wife, she's always telling me I need to go get a physical, get my blood pressure checked, all that standard stuff they tell you to do when you hit your fifties, but I just... I don't know, I never seem to make the time for it. So, no new medications, no old medications really, just me and my morning coffee... well, my three or four morning coffees, especially on those meeting days.

Thinking back to when you were a kid in school, did you have this same kind of restlessness—trouble sitting still, needing to move around—or is this something that's only started more recently in your adult life?

Oh, boy, back in school? Yeah, it's definitely not a new thing, doc. It goes way, way back. I mean, I remember being in, what was it, maybe third or fourth grade? Mrs. Gable's class, I think. I was always, always getting in trouble for just... popping right out of my seat. Like, I literally couldn't stay in the little wooden desk they had for us. I'd just stand up in the middle of a lesson because I felt like I had to stretch my legs or look out the window. And the talking, too. I was terrible about talking over the teacher. She'd be in the middle of explaining a math problem on the chalkboard—the old slate ones, you know, where the chalk dust would get everywhere—and I'd just blurt out the answer, or ask a question about something completely unrelated, like what we were having for lunch. 

And it wasn't just that, it was the rushing, too. I'd get a worksheet, and before she even finished reading the directions out loud to the class, I was already scribbling down answers, just trying to get it done as fast as humanly possible so I could go do something else, anything else. I got so many red marks for just missing the point of the assignment because I wouldn't wait to hear what we were actually supposed to do. My mother, God rest her soul, she used to say it all the time. She'd look at me running around the house, knocking things over, and she'd sigh and say, "You act like you're wound too tight, like a cheap pocket watch." She said I was like that even when I was a little bitty kid, just constantly humming with this energy that had to go somewhere. So, yeah, it's been a lifelong thing, this... this inability to just settle down and be still like a normal person. It's always been there, just under the surface, making me jump out of my skin.
Aside from the restlessness, do you often find yourself losing focus during tasks, forgetting things, or having trouble following through on details—both back in school and now at work?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because people always assume that if you're bouncing off the walls, you must be losing your mind, too, just forgetting everything. But honestly? No, not really. I mean, I don't think I have any more trouble focusing than the next guy. 

Take my job, for example. When I'm buffering those floors—and let me tell you, getting a good shine on the linoleum in the science building is an art form, it really is, because they track in all sorts of mud and whatever else from the quad—I am locked in. I don't miss a spot. I know exactly which chemicals to mix, how much water to use, what kind of pad the machine needs. I don't forget my keys, I don't leave closets unlocked, I don't skip steps. I'm actually pretty particular about it. My supervisor, Gary, he's been there for twenty years, and he always says my section of the building is the cleanest, because I don't miss the details. I might be doing it fast, and I might be sweating and moving a mile a minute, but I get it done right. 

And back in school... well, like I said, I was rushing. I'd miss the point of the assignment because I wouldn't wait for the instructions, sure. But if I actually knew what I was supposed to be doing? If it was something I could just dive into? I was fine. I wasn't sitting there daydreaming or losing my pencil or forgetting I even had homework. I just wanted to get it over with so I could go outside and ride my bike or build a fort in the woods behind our house. My brain wasn't floating away on a cloud, it was just... it was just driving a racecar, you know? I wanted to go, go, go. But as far as just spacing out or forgetting things? No, I wouldn't say that's me at all. My wife tells me I remember every slight and every conversation from the last thirty years, so my memory is sharp as a tack, doc. Just... a very fast-moving tack, I suppose.
Do you often find yourself worrying excessively about different things—like work, health, or family—even when there's no clear reason to be anxious?

Worrying? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, sure, I have the normal stuff, right? Like if the car makes a funny noise, I'll think, "Oh great, is the transmission going out again?" because I had a '98 Taurus that did that to me right before Christmas one year, and let me tell you, that was a nightmare trying to find a mechanic who was open and wouldn't charge an arm and a leg. But as far as just sitting around and stewing about things for no reason? No, no, I don't really do that. 

My wife, now, she's a worrier. She'll watch the evening news and then she can't sleep because she's thinking about the economy or what's happening halfway across the world, or she'll fret about our daughter's job, even though our daughter is doing just fine, she just got a promotion, actually, over at the bank. But me? I don't really have the time or the patience to just sit and fret. Like I said, I'm always on the move. If there's a problem, I want to fix it. If the sink is leaking, I'm under there with a wrench. I'm not going to sit at the kitchen table and wring my hands about water damage, you know? 

I guess my brain just doesn't work that way. It's too busy looking for the next thing to do. I don't get tied up in knots about my health either. Like I told you, I don't even go to the doctor much. I figure if something's really broken, my body will let me know, and until then, I'm just going to keep pushing the buffer and drinking my coffee. So, no, excessive worrying isn't really in my playbook. I just don't have the attention span for it, to be perfectly honest with you. I'd rather be doing something, anything, than just sitting there thinking about what-ifs.
